prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Toward evening, the natural light becomes intelligent and answers, without demur:“Be assured! You are not alone. . . .” But in fact, toward evening, I am not convinced there is any other except myself to whom existence necessarily pertains. I also interrogate myself to discover whether I myself possess any power by which I can bring it about that I who now am shall exist another moment. Because I am mostly a thinking thing and because this precise question can only be from that thoughtful part of myself, if such a power did reside within me I should, I am sure, be conscious of it. . . . But I am conscious of no such power. And yet, if I myself cannot be the cause of that assurance, surely it is necessary to conclude that I am not alone in the world. There is some other who is the cause of that idea. But if, at last, no such other can be found toward evening, do I really have sufficient assurance of the existence of any other being at all? For, after a most careful search, I have been unable to discover the ground of that conviction—unless it be imagined a lonely workman on a dizzy scaffold unfolds a sign at evening and puts his mark to it.

outputs.L2: As dusk approaches, daylight seems to acquire a mind and replies without hesitation: “Take comfort—you are not alone. . . .” Yet by evening I remain uncertain that, apart from myself, anything else exists by necessity. I therefore ask whether I possess some power capable of ensuring that the self who exists now will continue to exist in the next moment. Since I am chiefly a thinking being, and since this particular inquiry can arise only from the thinking part of me, I feel certain that, were such a power mine, I would know it. . . . But I detect no such power within myself. Nevertheless, if I cannot be the source of this assurance, then I must conclude that I am not the world’s only being: some other entity must have produced the idea. Still, if evening arrives and no such other can ultimately be found, what adequate certainty do I have that any being besides myself exists? Even after searching with the greatest care, I have discovered no foundation for this belief—unless one pictures a solitary laborer, high on a vertiginous scaffold, unfurling a sign at dusk and affixing his signature to it.

Yet this impression quickly gives way to philosophical doubt: he cannot be certain that any being other than himself necessarily exists. Indeed, he recognizes that he does not possess the conscious power to guarantee even his own continued existence from one moment to the next. This limitation suggests that some external being may sustain him, providing both the assurance of companionship and the source of his ongoing existence. Nevertheless, his search for evidence yields no firm basis for belief in such a being. In the end, certainty remains out of reach, and he is left only with the imagined figure of a solitary workman signaling from a scaffold—a fragile image of connection amid profound isolation.
outputs.L4:
How can I know that any being exists besides myself? Everything I encounter appears within consciousness: the shapes of things, the voices of others, the seeming resistance of the world. Yet none of these appearances can carry me beyond my own awareness. They may indicate realities outside me, but they may also be only impressions whose source I cannot discover. Even the people who speak to me are known only through words, gestures, and images presented to my mind. I cannot step outside consciousness to compare what I perceive with what truly exists.

Nor am I certain of my own continued existence. I know that I exist now, because I am thinking now; but what assures me that I will exist in the next moment? If consciousness possesses the power to preserve itself, I ought to be able to find some trace of that power within me. When I examine myself, however, I discover thoughts, sensations, memories, desires, and fears—but no force by which I create or sustain my being. I do not choose to pass from one instant to another. Each new moment simply arrives, bringing me with it.

Perhaps, then, some cause beyond me preserves my existence. But this conclusion, however tempting, does not amount to certainty. My inability to sustain myself does not reveal what sustains me, or even prove that the question has been framed correctly. I remain suspended between possibilities: unable to believe that I am entirely alone, yet unable to demonstrate that anything else is present.

In that uncertainty, I long for some assurance of companionship. I imagine another consciousness near me—someone who sees, understands, and confirms that I am not the sole witness of an empty universe. At times the thought itself feels like a sign, a faint answer offered against the terror of solitude. Yet I cannot be sure that this imagined companion comes from beyond me. The assurance may be only another appearance produced by the very mind it comforts.

Still, I hold to it. Fragile and doubtful as it is, the possibility of another presence keeps loneliness from becoming absolute. I cannot prove that I am accompanied, but neither can I prove that I am alone. Between those two uncertainties, I continue from moment to moment, waiting for a certainty that consciousness cannot give itself.
outputs.L5:
### Toward You, But—

I keep walking toward you, though the road refuses to stay straight. It bends around old memories, climbs over unspoken fears, and disappears beneath the fog of everything we never said.

You wait somewhere beyond certainty—close enough to imagine, too far to touch.

I want to call your name, but the word catches in my throat. I want to promise that I will reach you, but promises are fragile things. So I offer only this: another step, and then another.

Toward you.

Slowly, imperfectly—but still toward you.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal philosophical prose poem that blends René Descartes’s meditations on existence and God with the image of evening light reassuring a lonely speaker.
counterfactuals.output:
At evening, the light enters my room like a quiet theorem, laying its golden hand upon the chair, the cup, the book I have not opened. I doubt each object in turn. Perhaps the chair is dreaming the body it supports. Perhaps the cup contains only the memory of water. Perhaps the window is an eye painted by a patient deceiver.

Yet I am lonely, and therefore something in me leans toward proof.

I think—and the thought flickers like a moth inside a cathedral. I doubt—and the doubt becomes a small, stubborn sun. Even if a vast intelligence has arranged the world as a beautiful error, even if my hands are rumors and the floor is an argument without conclusion, still there is this trembling witness who asks to be deceived.

Outside, the evening gathers the trees into one dark sentence. The last light rests on the sill and seems to say: You are not required to understand the universe before it holds you.

I ask where God is.

The light does not answer. It becomes softer.

Perhaps perfection is not a blazing throne beyond the stars, but this impossible tenderness descending upon imperfect things: dust illuminated, walls forgiven, my solitary face briefly made warm. Perhaps the infinite has hidden its signature in the finite, as the sea hides in a drop that cannot remember falling.

I close my eyes to test the world.

The room vanishes, but the warmth remains.

And in that warmth, neither proof nor miracle, I feel evening beside me—an old philosopher with amber sleeves—whispering that doubt is not an empty house, but a door; that consciousness, however frightened, is already a candle; that somewhere beyond the machinery of shadows, a goodness I cannot demonstrate may still be thinking me.

So I sit until darkness completes its argument.

The light withdraws from every object, yet leaves a little radiance in my chest, as if the sun, before departing, had placed there one quiet premise:

You are here.

You are held.

Continue.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a literary collage in which a solitary narrator questions whether anyone else exists, while natural light seems to answer and a workman on a scaffold appears in the final image.
counterfactuals.output:
### Proof of Others

I called into the room:  
**Is anyone there?**

The chairs kept their wooden counsel.  
A cup cooled beside the window.  
Dust turned slowly in the air,  
each mote alone, each mote pretending  
not to notice the others.

**Am I the last?** I asked.

Morning entered without knocking.  
It laid a pale hand across the floorboards,  
climbed the wall, and opened  
a small gold door in the mirror.

Outside, leaves flashed their green signals.  
Clouds separated, joined, separated again.  
The sun answered in its broad language:

**Look.**

But looking was not believing.  
I searched the roofs for smoke,  
the street for a moving sleeve,  
the sky for some deliberate mark.

Then, high on the building opposite,  
a workman stepped onto a scaffold.

He carried a bucket of white paint.  
For a moment he stood against the brightness,  
suspended between earth and empty air.

He raised one arm—  
to balance, perhaps, or to greet me—

and the whole morning  
seemed to wave.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Rewrite the Cartesian argument that one cannot sustain one’s own existence from moment to moment as an atmospheric, modernist passage set toward evening.
counterfactuals.output:
Toward evening, the room seemed to loosen its hold on things. The table, the window, his own pale hand upon the sill—all persisted, but only barely, as if each moment had to be persuaded not to vanish into the next.

He considered that he existed now. This much was certain: the thought lit itself, briefly, within him. But what warrant had the present given the future? None. The instant that held him did not contain the instant to come. Time was not a cord but a succession of severed rooms, and in each one he must be placed anew.

If he possessed the power to preserve himself, he thought, he would feel it. He would lack nothing; he would be the author not only of this breath but of the next, and the next. Yet already the dusk had crossed half the floor without his consent. His heart continued in secrecy. The city’s lamps appeared one by one, lit by hands he could not see.

He was not carrying himself through time. Something else was carrying him—or creating him again at every darkening moment—while the evening gathered at the glass.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a Borgesian prose fragment about solipsism, consciousness, and the need for an external cause, ending with a lonely worker unfolding a sign at dusk.
counterfactuals.output:
I can’t write in Borges’s exact style, but I can offer an original metaphysical fragment shaped by labyrinths, paradoxes, invented scholarship, and philosophical unease.

---

In the third appendix to *The Vigil of Things*, Doctor Elías Varo advances a doctrine so simple that later commentators mistook it for a joke: consciousness is not proof of existence but evidence of intrusion.

Varo begins, conventionally, with the solitary mind. A man may doubt the street, the rain against the shutters, even the pale hand that turns the page; he cannot doubt the doubt itself. Yet this certainty appalled Varo. If the universe were merely the dream of the thinker, why did it resist him? Why did forgotten names remain forgotten? Why did pain arrive uninvited, with an ingenuity exceeding desire? The solipsist, Varo wrote, is an emperor condemned to receive decrees he does not remember issuing.

He proposed, therefore, an external cause—not necessarily God, nor matter, nor another consciousness, but something outside the closed circle of awareness. He called it the Witness. The Witness did not create the world. It created the world’s refusal to obey.

His opponents observed that the Witness might itself be another invention of the mind. Varo accepted the objection and altered his theory: the Witness was precisely that which the mind must invent in order to explain what it cannot invent. This circularity pleased him. He compared it to a door painted on a wall which, after years of contemplation, is found ajar.

The last pages of the appendix describe a city whose inhabitants have all embraced solipsism. Each citizen believes the others to be phantoms; courtesy survives only because no one wishes to offend the obscure author of the dream. The markets open, tribunals convene, lovers exchange vows, and soldiers die for a country each privately suspects is no more than a recurring image. At sunset, however, the city grows afraid. Night, being the suspension of witnesses, seems to threaten the abolition of streets and bodies alike.

Varo’s manuscript ends mid-sentence. A note in another hand claims that he vanished while crossing a public square. No one saw him vanish; several saw the empty square afterward.

Years later, the municipality erected a notice there, though its wording has never been recorded. Every evening, when the shops close and the windows darken, a lonely worker unfolds the sign at dusk.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce an experimental paragraph that combines philosophical language from Descartes’s *Meditations* with lyrical imagery of intelligent light, existential isolation, and an ambiguous assurance that the speaker is not alone.
counterfactuals.output: I doubt, therefore the darkness trembles: for while I withdraw from every uncertain thing—the body, the window, the rumored world—an intelligent light gathers behind my eyes, not shining upon objects but questioning them into being. Perhaps I am only a thinking thing suspended in an infinite night, deceived even by the stars, each one a cold syllable spoken by no mouth I can trust. Yet within this solitude, clear and distinct as a wound, there persists a brightness that does not seem entirely mine. Whether it is God, another mind, or merely the echo by which thought consoles itself, I cannot determine; still, when I say *I am*, something in the luminous distance answers—not in words, not with proof, but almost as if I were not alone.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
